insight.title: Why we all live inside the same clock
insight.subtitle: The moment time stopped being local and became a machine

sections.text: Before the trains, every village lived by its own sun. High noon in London was several minutes away from high noon in Bristol. People preferred the slow, messy rhythm of their shadows. But as steam engines began to race across the land, these tiny gaps in time became deadly, invisible walls between rushing iron wheels.

To keep engines from colliding, we had to flatten the world. Stations wired their clocks together, forcing hundreds of different "noons" into a single, artificial heartbeat. It was a silent revolution of the wrist. Suddenly, time was no longer a gift from the sky, but a strict schedule dictated by the rhythmic clicking of copper wires.

We traded our unique, solar mornings for a global synchronization that allows us to meet across oceans. This efficiency built the modern world, yet it also disconnected us from our immediate surroundings. We stopped looking up at the light to know the hour. Now, we carry the ghost of those Victorian railway tracks in every digital pocket.
We did not master time; we simply agreed to let it rule us together.

news.title: "Is US sure it wants to turn back clock?" Iran FM's jibe at Trump's 'Stone Age' remark
news.description: Iranian leaders have strongly criticized Donald Trump's threats to devastate Iran. Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi questioned the logic of such actions. President Masoud Pezeshkian highlighted Iran's peaceful history and condemned attacks on medical facilities. Parliament Speaker MB Ghalibaf suggested financial motives behind the policy. These statements come amid rising global concerns over energy security.
news.why: Increased war risks could significantly raise your monthly fuel and energy bills.

news.title: For some around Trump, war on Iran is a Christian calling
news.description: Religion is playing a role in the US conflict with Iran. President Donald Trump has met with Christian pastors who offered blessings. Some officials view the conflict as a divine mission. This echoes historical religious wars. Iran's government is also religiously rooted. The US is invoking religious themes in its foreign policy.
news.why: Global conflict may lead to higher travel costs and flight disruptions.

news.title: Boost to small exporters, MSMEs as govt removes Rs 10
news.description: In a significant policy shift aimed at boosting exports and easing trade processes, the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, through the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT), has removed the existing ₹10 lakh per-consignment value cap on exports made through courier services. The amendment, notified under the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992, will come into force from April 1, 2026.
news.why: You might find more job opportunities at local small businesses and exporters.

These restrictions will apply irrespective of any prior contract, irrevocable letter of credit, advance payment, shipment status, or any other commitment, the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) said in a notification. news.title: Akhilesh Yadav Criticizes BJP, Urges Return to Ballot Voting
news.description: Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav criticized the BJP for blaming domestic problems on foreign conflicts such as the Iran-Israel clash. He addressed industrial concerns in Kanpur, farmer issues, and advocated for returning to ballot voting. Yadav also discussed student politics and India's foreign policy stance.
news.why: The actual process of how you cast your vote may change.

news.title: Opinion | Why India’s Discretion Trumps Grandstanding In West Asia
news.description: There is wisdom in eschewing heroics for discretion in an escalating war theatre. Indian foreign policy has come a long way from effete non-alignment to deliberate detachment.
news.why: Careful diplomacy helps keep your local fuel and energy prices stable.

news.title: U.S. Lifts Sanctions on Noted Russian Banker Mikhail Zadornov
news.description: The U.S. has lifted sanctions against Mikhail Zadornov, a prominent Russian banker and former finance minister. Despite the delisting, there is no broader shift in U.S. policy towards Russian sanctions. Zadornov's removal results from a successful petition to the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control.
news.why: Transferring money internationally or using global banks may become easier.
